original_question: For regular closed curves in R^n equipped with their orthonormal Frenet frames in O(n), is the length of the Frenet frame always strictly greater than mu(n) times the length of the standard closed geodesic SO(2) embedded in O(n), where mu(n) is the minimum multiplicity needed for a plane convex curve to admit a regular perturbation in R^n?
target_in_paper: Section VI, "Closed curves with a nondegenerate Frenet frame": the unnumbered open problem asking to determine μ(n) for n > 3 and to decide whether every closed nondegenerate curve in R^n has Frenet-frame length strictly larger than μ(n) times the length of the shortest closed geodesic SO(2) ⊂ O(n).
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the paper's Section VI problem about closed curves in R^n, their orthonormal Frenet frames as closed curves in O(n), the comparison with the standard SO(2) closed geodesic, and the role of μ(n) as the minimal winding multiplicity connected with perturbing convex plane curves into nondegenerate curves in higher-dimensional Euclidean space.
missing_details: The paper's open problem has two linked parts: not only the lower bound for Frenet-frame length, but also the determination of μ(n) for n > 3.
The ambient objects are smooth closed curves γ:S^1→R^n.

The relevant class is really closed nondegenerate curves: the paper defines degeneracy by γ̇(t) ∧ ··· ∧ γ^(n)(t) = 0, and only nondegenerate curves admit the closed orthonormal Frenet frame E:S^1→O(n).
Your draft should make explicit that μ(n) is defined using an m-fold traversal of a convex plane closed curve, not a single traversal in general.
The perturbation in the definition of μ(n) is a small perturbation in R^n of that m-times-run convex plane curve; the paper's wording is "regular small perturbations."
The comparison length is measured in O(n) with its standard bi-invariant metric.
The reference SO(2) ⊂ O(n) is the shortest closed geodesic, equivalently the Frenet frame of a plane convex curve viewed inside R^n.
The paper records the known base cases μ(2)=1 and μ(3)=2, so the unresolved part is specifically for n > 3.
The motivating three-dimensional case is already known: in R^3 the length of the Frenet frame of any regular curve is greater than twice the length of SO(2).

Section VI immediately gives a control-theoretic reformulation via the Frenet structural equations; while not necessary in the final question, it is part of the paper's intended framing and explains why the problem is posed this way.
refined_question: For each n > 3, determine μ(n), the smallest positive integer m such that an m-fold traversal of a smooth closed convex plane curve admits a small nondegenerate perturbation as a closed curve in R^n, where nondegenerate means that γ̇(t) ∧ ··· ∧ γ^(n)(t) ≠ 0 for all t ∈ S^1; and decide whether every smooth closed nondegenerate curve γ:S^1→R^n, with orthonormal Frenet frame E:S^1→O(n), satisfies Len(E) > μ(n)·Len(SO(2)), where SO(2) ⊂ O(n) is the standard shortest closed geodesic (with O(n) equipped with its standard bi-invariant metric).
equivalent_formulation: Equivalent control-theoretic formulation from Section VI: regular closed curves together with their Frenet frames are periodic admissible trajectories of the Frenet system (1) with positive controls, and the problem is to identify the shortest periodic trajectory in this class; in this language, μ(n) is the least m for which the trajectory corresponding to the m-times-run circle admits a small positive perturbation that remains periodic.
justification: The draft is clearly aiming at the unnumbered open problem in Section VI rather than any numbered conjecture or theorem elsewhere in the paper. Section VI first defines degenerate/nondegenerate closed curves and their Frenet frames, then states the known n=3 comparison with 2·Len(SO(2)), and finally formulates the actual open problem as: find μ(n) for n>3 and check whether the Frenet-frame length of any regular curve in R^n is greater than μ(n) times the length of SO(2) ⊂ O(n). The same section immediately reformulates the question in optimal-control terms via the Frenet equations, so the alternate formulation above is paper-faithful.
